name: Anthony Bennett
notes: Undersized, powerfully built UNLV forward who won Mountain West Freshman of the Year (16.1/8.1) on pure explosiveness attacking the rim. Cleveland's decision to take him 1st overall was a surprise even at the time — Nerlens Noel was the presumptive top pick — and evaluators were already flagging real uncertainty about what position Bennett would even play in the league. That uncertainty proved fatal: he never found a role on either end, bounced from Cleveland to Minnesota to Toronto to Brooklyn in barely three years, and was out of the NBA and playing overseas well before his rookie contract would have expired. Still regarded as one of the most complete draft busts at the very top of a draft in league history.

name: Victor Oladipo
notes: Indiana off-guard drafted 2nd on elite two-way athleticism — a defensive menace and open-floor finisher whose jumper was still coming together (three-point mark jumped from 20.8% to 44.1% in his final college season). The tools translated fully once he landed in the right situation: traded to Indiana in 2017, Oladipo won Most Improved Player, made his first All-Star team, led the league in steals, and made All-Defensive First Team and All-NBA — a legitimate star-level peak that validated the pre-draft billing. But a ruptured quad tendon in January 2019 started a chain of setbacks (two quad surgeries, then a ruptured patellar tendon in the 2023 playoffs) that he never fully came back from. Solid rather than Hit: the ceiling was real and briefly realized, but the healthy stretch was too short to bank as a true career hit.

name: Otto Porter Jr.
notes: Georgetown wing who broke out as a sophomore into a do-everything, no-weakness 3-and-D profile: 7'1" wingspan, above-average across the board rather than elite in any one area, taken 3rd by Washington. The NBA career matched the scouting report almost exactly — eleven seasons, career averages of 10.7/5.0/1.4 on 39.9% from three, valued everywhere he went for exactly the length-plus-spacing skill set scouts identified, capped by a title run with Golden State in 2022. Solid outcome: he became precisely the long-career 3-and-D role player projected, never more, never less.

name: Cody Zeller
notes: Indiana big man whose blend of skill, mobility and feel for a seven-footer drew real Pau Gasol comparisons pre-draft, taken 4th by Charlotte; the flagged weakness was finishing through length with unusually short arms for his size. That trade-off defined a long, useful career rather than a star one — All-Rookie Second Team, eight seasons anchoring Charlotte's frontcourt as a switchable screen-and-roll big, later stops in Portland and Miami (including a 2023 Finals run). Solid outcome: exactly the skilled-but-limited-length role big the scouts described, never the plus rim protector his size alone might have suggested.

name: Alex Len
notes: Maryland center with prototypical physical tools — a true 7'1" frame and 7'3.5" wingspan, mobile and capable of face-up jumpers out to 15 feet — taken 5th by Phoenix. The scouting question was passivity: whether he'd assert himself enough to use those tools consistently. It was the right question. Len never developed into a full-time NBA starter, instead settling in as a journeyman backup center through stops with Phoenix, Sacramento, Atlanta and Washington — solid rim-runner minutes, never the two-way anchor the physical profile promised. Bust relative to a top-5 selection: the tools never translated into an every-night role.

name: Nerlens Noel
notes: Kentucky center whose elite length, foot speed and shot-blocking instincts (10.5/9.5/4.4 blk before a season-ending ACL tear) drew lofty Anthony Davis comparisons — length and athleticism matched, but evaluators were already flagging that he lacked anything resembling Davis's offensive skill. Taken 6th by New Orleans and immediately dealt to Philadelphia for Jrue Holiday, Noel had a genuinely strong defensive stretch early (9.9/8.1/1.9 blk as a 76er), but chronic injuries wore him down across a decade in the league, and his career averages settled at a modest 7.1/6.1/1.1 — a steep fall from a prospect once talked about in top-two-pick terms. Bust: the offensive limitation scouts flagged never resolved, and injuries compounded it.

name: Ben McLemore
notes: Kansas shooting guard with textbook off-guard tools — 6'5", explosive above the rim, a knockdown shooter (42% from three, Ray Allen comps) taken 7th by Sacramento. The red flag pre-draft was consistency: he'd disappear for stretches and needed to be more assertive, evaluators calling him a true boom-or-bust bet. That's exactly how it played out — McLemore never developed into a full-time, reliable scoring option, drifting through Sacramento, Memphis, Houston and other stops as a streaky specialist rather than the plus-shooter wing his tools suggested. Bust: the exact mental-approach concern flagged pre-draft is what capped the career.

name: Kentavious Caldwell-Pope
notes: Georgia's SEC Player of the Year (18.5/7.1), drafted 8th by Detroit on a translatable, no-frills two-way shooting guard profile — long arms, deep NBA range on a quick catch-and-shoot release, and a defensive-stud reputation coming out of college. The NBA career is close to a direct match: a long run as a plus perimeter defender and reliable movement shooter, valuable enough to be a key rotation piece on two championship teams (Lakers 2020, Nuggets 2023). Solid outcome: hit the exact translatable skill set scouts projected and built a genuinely winning career around it, without ever becoming an offensive engine in his own right.

name: Trey Burke
notes: Michigan's national Player of the Year after a title-game run, an undersized (6'1", plus a long 6'5" wingspan) but crafty lead guard with a Tony Parker comp attached — deadly first step, mature feel, capable scoring or creating. Drafted 9th by Minnesota and immediately dealt to Utah on draft night, Burke never developed into that floor-general archetype; instead he became a journeyman combo guard through Utah, Washington, New York, Dallas and Philadelphia, settling into a instant-offense bench-scorer role (career 9.6/3.1/1.8) rather than a starting point guard. Bust relative to the top-5 college billing, though he carved out a real, lasting NBA living as a reserve.

name: CJ McCollum
notes: Lehigh's all-time leading scorer, a 6'3" combo guard who averaged 19+ points in all four college seasons but carried real small-school-competition skepticism into the draft, going 10th to Portland. McCollum became one of the genuine value picks of the class: a legitimate go-to scorer who built a long partnership alongside Damian Lillard in Portland's backcourt, finishing with career averages around 19.5 points per game across 800+ regular-season appearances, before later moves to New Orleans (2022), Washington (2025), and Atlanta (Jan. 2026). Hit outcome: dramatically outproduced the pedigree concerns that dropped him to the back of the lottery.

name: Michael Carter-Williams
notes: Syracuse's pass-first floor general, a 6'6" point guard with the size to see over defenses and finish top-3 nationally in assists. Scouts liked the size-skill combo but were already nervous about the jumper — even his best college season showed real efficiency red flags. Drafted 11th by Philadelphia, Carter-Williams won Rookie of the Year (16.7/6.2/6.3), joining Oscar Robertson and Magic Johnson in that stat club. But the flagged weakness never got fixed: he shot roughly 20% on jumpers even in his award-winning rookie year, and four straight seasons of decline followed as defenses simply sagged off him. Bust: a genuine ROY-caliber debut collapsed almost entirely because the one skill scouts doubted never arrived.

name: Steven Adams
notes: One-and-done Pittsburgh center, 12th overall to Oklahoma City — huge physical tools (7'5" wingspan, 255 lb frame, a genuine motor and 2.0 blocks/game) paired with about as raw an offensive game as a lottery big man can have, described as lacking the footwork and hands to score down low. The Thunder never needed him to develop a scoring game: Adams became one of the league's premier screen-setters, offensive rebounders and interior physical presences for over a decade, a foundational piece of multiple playoff Thunder and Rockets teams. Hit outcome: the exact high-motor, defense-and-glass big projected pre-draft, just far more durable and impactful than a typical 12th pick.

name: Kelly Olynyk
notes: Late-blooming Gonzaga big who barely played his first two college seasons before returning from a redshirt year 30 pounds heavier and transformed into an All-American — an unusually skilled 7-footer with real perimeter touch and ball-handling thanks to a background as a point guard, but a poor shot-blocker and clear defensive/athleticism liability. Taken 13th by Dallas and immediately dealt to Boston, Olynyk became exactly the skilled offensive stretch big projected, if never much of a defender: a long, valuable NBA career spanning Boston, Miami (a 2020 Finals trip), Houston, Detroit, Utah, Toronto, New Orleans and San Antonio. Solid outcome: a real rotation-caliber stretch five for over a decade, capped by the defensive limitations flagged pre-draft.

name: Shabazz Muhammad
notes: UCLA wing who entered the year projected as a top-3 pick alongside Nerlens Noel but underwhelmed scouts with poor rebounding and steal numbers, sub-1 assist per game, and a reputation around the league for being ball-dominant and unselfish only in name. Fell to 14th (Utah). The NBA career tracked those red flags closely — Muhammad never developed a role beyond streaky bench scoring, finishing with modest career averages (9.0/2.8/0.5) and out of the league by 2018. Bust: the same one-dimensional, low-feel profile scouts worried about at UCLA is exactly what capped him as a pro.

name: Giannis Antetokounmpo
notes: An 18-year-old playing in Greece's second division, largely unknown to American scouts, but flagged for rare physical tools: 6'9" with a reported 7'3" wingspan and the mobility to play multiple positions — evaluators called him perhaps the draft's biggest mystery and expected a multi-year draft-and-stash project. Milwaukee took him 15th anyway. What followed is one of the great outlier outcomes in draft history: Giannis grew another 2.5 inches as a rookie, developed into a two-time MVP and Defensive Player of the Year (only the third player ever to win both in the same season, alongside Jordan and Olajuwon), and led the Bucks to the 2021 championship. Hit, in the most extreme sense the tag allows — a draft-and-stash flier who became a top-5 player in the sport.

name: Lucas Nogueira
notes: Brazilian big man taken 16th (Boston, draft-rights traded to Atlanta then Toronto) on projection alone — a 7-footer with a 7'6" wingspan, a runner's motor, and shot-blocking instincts, but a raw, unpolished offensive game and only limited minutes overseas to evaluate. The Raptors kept him as a stash/development project for a year before his debut, and he settled into exactly the low-usage rim-protecting reserve role scouts described: four seasons in Toronto, 141 games, modest per-minute production (3.2/2.8/1.0 blk in 12.4 min) on efficient close-range shooting. Bust relative to a first-round selection — never developed the offensive polish to play meaningful minutes, and left the NBA in his mid-20s for Spain.

name: Dennis Schröder
notes: German lead guard who rocketed from projected second-rounder to late lottery/mid-first after a strong Nike Hoops Summit — a strong-armed, blur-quick 6'2" point guard who shot 40.2% from three in Germany, drawing (overly optimistic) Rajon Rondo comps that scouts tempered down to Ramon Sessions. Atlanta took him 17th. The NBA version outpaced even the tempered comp: Schroder became a long-tenured, high-mileage starting-caliber guard across a 13-year career and counting (Hawks, Thunder, Lakers, Celtics, Rockets, Raptors, Nets, Warriors, Pistons, Kings, Cavaliers, now Charlotte), and captained Germany to the 2023 FIBA World Cup title. Solid outcome: never a star, but a durable, always-employable starting or high-minutes guard for well over a decade.

name: Shane Larkin
notes: Undersized (5'11", 171 lb) but explosive Miami point guard — fastest sprint and second-highest vertical (44") at the combine — whose speed and shooting carried an ACC title run, with defense flagged as the clear question mark given his size. Taken 18th (Atlanta, traded to Dallas). The NBA career confirmed the size concern: a modest 256-game run with Dallas, New York, Brooklyn and Boston (5.5/2.9 assists), never a full-time rotation piece. But Larkin found a second, much better career overseas — a fixture with Anadolu Efes (and now Fenerbahce) in Turkey, winning multiple EuroLeague and Turkish titles, an All-EuroLeague First Team selection, and a 49-point EuroLeague game. Bust as an NBA prospect, but a legitimate European star.

name: Sergey Karasev
notes: Russian wing with legitimate size for the position (6'7") and a track record scoring efficiently in top-level European competition, taken 19th by Cleveland — evaluators loved the shot-making pedigree but flagged an average wingspan, below-average athleticism, and an undersized frame that would need added strength before he could hold up defensively in the NBA. Those defensive concerns proved decisive: Karasev lasted only two brief NBA stints (Cleveland, then Brooklyn) before returning to Russia, where he's played out the rest of a long career as a respected VTB League scorer and, now, team captain for Zenit Saint Petersburg. Bust at the NBA level — the exact defensive limitation flagged pre-draft never let him stick in a rotation.

name: Tony Snell
notes: New Mexico wing with prototypical 3-and-D measurables — 6'7" with a massive 6'11.5" wingspan, a clean catch-and-shoot stroke (39% from three as a junior) and solid on-ball defensive tools — but scouts flagged him as purely a catch-and-shoot player who struggled putting the ball on the floor and rebounded poorly for his size. Chicago took him 20th. The NBA career landed almost exactly on that projection: a long run (Bulls, Bucks, Pistons, Hawks, Trail Blazers, Pelicans) as a low-usage floor-spacing wing defender, never asked to do more than the scouting report said he could. Solid outcome: precisely the limited-but-useful 3-and-D wing scouts described.

name: Gorgui Dieng
notes: Louisville's Big East Defensive Player of the Year and a key piece of the Cardinals' 2013 national title team — a 7'4"-wingspan rim protector and switchable pick-and-roll defender who also flashed real passing and mid-range touch, with the main question being limited offensive upside given his age (turning 24 as a rookie). Utah took him 21st and immediately dealt him to Minnesota for Trey Burke. Dieng validated the profile almost immediately, posting the first 20-point, 20-rebound game by a rookie in Timberwolves history, and carved out a long career as a rock-solid rotation big (Minnesota, Memphis, San Antonio) valued for exactly the shot-blocking, passing and switchability scouts flagged. Solid outcome: a durable, high-IQ frontcourt piece for over a decade.

name: Mason Plumlee
notes: Duke senior big who broke out as a highly efficient (59.9% FG) roll man and elite screen-setter, an explosive leaper with great hands but a wingspan that ran shorter than his height and essentially no perimeter shot — scouts pegged him as a mid-first-round, rim-only reserve big. Brooklyn took him 22nd. That's almost exactly the career he had, if a longer and more useful one than projected: a well-traveled, high-IQ passing/screening/rolling center across Brooklyn, Portland, Denver, Detroit, Charlotte and the Clippers, valued everywhere for the same rim-finishing and playmaking-from-the-five skills identified at Duke. Solid outcome: a durable journeyman starter/rotation big exactly within his scouted limitations.

name: Solomon Hill
notes: Arizona's do-it-all senior wing (13.4/5.3 on 45.8% shooting), praised for basketball IQ, anticipation, and the handle/vision to play some point guard — Indiana's front office specifically cited his defensive film grading out as terrific, comping him to a Jared Dudley type. His first-round selection at 23rd overall was considered a mild reach at the time. The NBA career mostly matched that modest, glue-guy billing: a nine-year run (Pacers, Pelicans, Grizzlies, Heat, Hawks) as a low-usage, switchable wing defender and occasional starter, never more than a role piece. Mixed outcome: he carved out a legitimately long NBA career on his defensive versatility, but never developed enough offensive juice to be more than replacement-level, and the pick was seen as a reach even at the time.

name: Tim Hardaway Jr.
notes: Michigan's second-leading scorer as a junior (14.5/4.7/2.4), a prototypically sized off-guard (6'5") who could stretch the floor and finish above the rim, but scouts flagged real jump-shot inconsistency he'd need to iron out to earn a rotation spot. New York took him 24th. Hardaway did iron it out — he developed into a legitimate, high-volume knockdown shooter, most notably during long stints with Atlanta and then Dallas (where he was a full-time starter and double-digit scorer for five seasons), before later moves to Detroit, Denver and Miami. Solid outcome: the inconsistent shooter scouts worried about became one of the more reliable movement shooters of his draft class, without ever reaching star level.

name: Reggie Bullock
notes: UNC's third-leading scorer as a junior and the class's second-best 3-point-shooting small forward, hitting 43.6% from three on real volume (5.8 attempts/game) with a defensive profile scouts liked just as much as the shooting. The Clippers took him 25th. Bullock became precisely that translatable 3-and-D wing at the NBA level — a long career (Clippers, Pistons, Lakers, Knicks, Mavericks and beyond) as a reliable catch-and-shoot floor-spacer and switchable defender, never a star but a steady rotation fixture for over a decade. Solid outcome: hit the shooting-plus-defense translation almost exactly as projected.

name: Andre Roberson
notes: Colorado wing who surprised by going in the first round (26th, to Minnesota then dealt to OKC) on a defense-only profile: Pac-12 Defensive Player of the Year, elite length and motor, but visibly uncomfortable creating with the ball and no perimeter shot to speak of. The NBA version of Roberson matched the scouting report almost beat for beat — he became a four-year Thunder starter and one of the league's premier perimeter defenders, drawing All-Defensive and DPOY buzz while guarding the opponent's best wing alongside the Westbrook/George core. The offensive limitation never resolved (career 46.8% from the line, no jumper ever developed), and in January 2018 he ruptured his patellar tendon — a brutal, 30-month recovery riddled with setbacks that cost him his explosiveness and, ultimately, his NBA career. Mixed outcome: he hit the defensive ceiling scouts projected at an elite level, but the offensive cap plus a catastrophic injury cut off what looked like a longer run as a championship-level 3-and-D piece.

name: Rudy Gobert
notes: French big man whose draft stock was built entirely on measurements scouts called unprecedented — a 7'2" frame with a 7'9" wingspan — plus real defensive playmaking at the rim, with the obvious question being whether any offensive game existed beyond put-backs and lobs. Denver took him 27th and immediately dealt him to Utah. Gobert became the extreme-outlier version of that profile: a 4x Defensive Player of the Year, 3x All-Star, and 8x All-Defensive First Teamer who redefined how much value a non-scoring center could provide. Hit, at a level almost no one projected from a 27th pick.

name: Livio Jean-Charles
notes: French forward (ASVEL) taken 28th by San Antonio off measurables and energy — a long (7'2" wingspan), high-motor slasher and put-back threat who was named MVP of the 2013 Nike Hoop Summit, but arrived with essentially no perimeter offensive skill. The Spurs never actually brought him into their rotation; he didn't make the NBA roster after returning from France and spent his entire pro career in the G League and, mostly, overseas. Bust: a stash pick whose offensive limitations kept him out of an NBA box score entirely.

name: Archie Goodwin
notes: Kentucky's leading scorer as a freshman (14.1 ppg) but shooting an alarming 26.6% from three, an explosive, high-upside wing whose evaluators flatly called not NBA-ready — the youngest American in the field with an inconsistent jumper that never got fixed. Drafted 29th (Thunder, traded to Phoenix), Goodwin lived out that scouting report: a brief NBA run as a marginal bench piece (6.3/2.0/1.2 career) before falling out of the league. Bust: the shooting question flagged at 19 years old was never answered.

name: Nemanja Nedović
notes: Serbian combo guard nicknamed the "European Derrick Rose" for a 41-inch vertical and blur-quick first step, but scouts were explicit that his assist-to-turnover profile made him a scorer without a clear position, unlikely to stick as a lead guard. Phoenix took him 30th and dealt him to Golden State. That positional question sank the NBA career before it started — a token 1.1/0.6/0.5 across a handful of games before he was out of the league by 2014 and back to a long, productive career in Europe. Bust at the NBA level: elite athleticism with no translatable offensive role.

name: Allen Crabbe
notes: Cal's 2013 Pac-12 Player of the Year, a long (6'11" wingspan) catch-and-shoot two-guard whose entire pre-draft case was a picture-perfect jumper with NBA range — not an explosive athlete, but a proven, high-volume shooter. Cleveland took him 31st and traded him to Portland. Crabbe became precisely that translatable shooting specialist at the NBA level: a steady four-team, 381-game career averaging 9.1 points on 38.9% from three. Solid outcome: the shooting-first profile scouted at Cal is exactly what carried an eight-plus-year NBA career.

name: Álex Abrines
notes: 19-year-old Spanish wing (FC Barcelona) taken 32nd by Oklahoma City as a pure draft-and-stash — at the time of the pick he was playing only 10 minutes a game for Barça, with three years of development in Spain assumed before any NBA look. He used that runway exactly as intended, developing into a 40%-plus EuroLeague three-point shooter before signing with the Thunder in 2016. The NBA version was a solid if limited three-and-D specialist (5.3 ppg, 35% from three across 174 games) before injuries and personal issues cut the run short in 2019. Mixed outcome: the draft-and-stash plan worked exactly as designed, but the NBA stay itself was brief and unremarkable.

name: Carrick Felix
notes: Arizona State's most-improved-player-caliber senior wing, a 6'6" high-motor athlete (38.5" vertical) who profiled purely as a defend-and-finish role player with little shot creation to his game. Cleveland took him 33rd. The NBA career never got past bit-part minutes — a brief run (2.7/0.9/0.6) that ended by 2014. Bust relative to a first-round selection: the limited offensive skill set scouted at Arizona State left no path to a real NBA role.

name: Isaiah Canaan
notes: Murray State's four-year floor general, a 6'0" combo guard who finished 6th in the country in scoring as a senior (22.4 ppg) on the strength of deep range and pull-up shot-making, but scouts flagged real size and pick-and-roll defense concerns and questioned whether he could shift from scorer to true point guard. Houston took him 34th. Canaan carved out a real journeyman NBA career (Rockets, 76ers, Bulls, Suns, Timberwolves, Bucks) as exactly the instant-offense microwave scorer projected, without ever solving the defensive limitations that capped him below a starting role. Mixed outcome: a legitimately long NBA bench career built on the one skill scouts trusted, capped by the one they didn't.

name: Glen Rice Jr.
notes: Son of the Hall of Famer, a knockdown shooter (6'6", ~40" vertical, huge wingspan) whose path to the draft ran through a dismissal from Georgia Tech and a D-League Finals MVP-caliber run with Rio Grande Valley rather than a normal college season — real shooting talent, real off-court red flags. Philadelphia took him 35th and dealt him to Washington. The red flags won out: Rice appeared in just 16 total NBA games (2.7/1.5) before disappearing from the league entirely. Bust: talent that never got a real chance to show up in an NBA box score.

name: Ray McCallum
notes: Detroit Mercy point guard (playing for his own father) who improved every college season, finishing with an 18.7/5.1/4.5 senior year and a diverse, low-turnover offensive game, but evaluators flagged inconsistent outside shooting and only average physical tools as the ceiling-cappers. Sacramento took him 36th. McCallum's NBA career matched that modest profile closely — four seasons as a fringe backup guard, never developing the outside shot that scouts doubted. Mixed outcome: a real, multi-year NBA roster spot, but never more than deep-bench depth exactly as projected.

name: Tony Mitchell
notes: North Texas forward regarded pre-draft as maybe the most explosive pound-for-pound athlete in the class (7'2.5" wingspan, 38" vertical, elite shot-blocking rate) after a double-double freshman season alongside Anthony Davis nationally — but he regressed badly as a sophomore following a coaching change, and that inconsistency is exactly what scouts couldn't get past. Detroit took him 37th anyway on pure upside. The bet didn't pay off: Mitchell played just 21 NBA games (1.0 ppg) before disappearing from the league. Bust: the sophomore-year regression that worried scouts turned out to be the real player.

name: Nate Wolters
notes: South Dakota State's four-year engine, a genuine pass-first playmaker (22.3/5.8/5.6 as a senior, third-team All-American) with a reliable perimeter shot, but flagged for below-average NBA athleticism and real concerns about foot speed and strength on defense. Washington took him 38th and dealt him to Philadelphia (for Glen Rice Jr.). The athletic limitations proved decisive at the NBA level — two seasons with Milwaukee as a fringe backup before the career shifted overseas, where Wolters played out a long, productive international career. Bust as an NBA prospect, useful pro elsewhere.

name: Jeff Withey
notes: Kansas's defensive anchor as a senior, setting a Big 12 career blocks record and an NCAA tournament blocks record (31 in the 2013 tournament) — elite rim-protection instincts paired with almost no offensive game beyond point-blank finishes (14 total jumpers attempted his senior year). Portland took him 39th. Withey became exactly the specialist projected: five NBA seasons as a low-usage, shot-blocking backup center before finishing out his career overseas from 2017 on. Mixed outcome: he found a real NBA role playing to his one elite skill, but never developed enough offense to be more than deep reserve depth.

name: Grant Jerrett
notes: Arizona one-and-done who was actually a consensus top-100 recruit coming out of high school but had a disappointing freshman year (5.2/3.6) — scouts already flagging him as awkward, unathletic and one of the draft's worst rebounding bigs despite real touch as a stretch four. Portland took him 40th (rights dealt to OKC) purely on shooting projection. That gamble didn't pay off: Jerrett played just eight total NBA games across three seasons, spending the rest in the G League. Bust: the athleticism and rebounding concerns flagged pre-draft left no NBA role for the shooting skill alone.

name: Jamaal Franklin
notes: San Diego State's do-everything junior (Mountain West Player of the Year, led the team in scoring/assists/rebounds/steals) with a Kawhi-Leonard-caliber physical profile — a 6'11" wingspan on a 6'5" frame — but scouts flagged real defensive engagement issues, noting he often looked disinterested guarding the perimeter. Memphis took him 41st. The engagement question proved fatal: Franklin lasted only two NBA seasons (Grizzlies, Nuggets) as a fringe reserve (1.8/1.0/0.4) before falling out of the league. Bust: elite tools undone by exactly the effort/engagement concern scouts raised.

name: Pierre Jackson
notes: Baylor's undersized (5'10.5") but electric lead guard — first ever to lead the Big 12 in scoring and assists in the same season, a knockdown shooter off the dribble or catch — with size and standing reach flagged as potentially the smallest ever to stick in the NBA. Philadelphia took him 42nd and immediately dealt him to New Orleans in the Nerlens Noel trade. The size concern won out: Jackson never played an NBA regular-season game, instead setting the G League single-game scoring record (58 points) and building a long, decorated career overseas and in the G League. Bust at the NBA level despite legitimate pro-caliber scoring talent.

name: Ricky Ledo
notes: A former five-star recruit who never played a college game — ruled academically ineligible at Providence and evaluated purely off practices — with obvious size and shot-creation upside but inconsistent shooting mechanics and a total lack of game reps against real competition. Milwaukee took him 43rd (rights traded to Dallas) on that pure talent bet. The lack of seasoning showed: Ledo appeared in just six total NBA games (1.2 ppg) before the run ended. Bust: the total absence of a proven track record scouts worried about never got resolved in the pros either.

name: Mike Muscala
notes: Bucknell stretch big regarded as one of the draft's sleepers — a 6'11" senior who led all Combine participants in spot-up shooting and shot 50%+ from the floor for three straight seasons, with added NBA range projected as the swing skill. Dallas took him 44th and dealt him to Atlanta. Muscala became exactly that translatable floor-spacing five, developing a real NBA three-point shot and carving out a decade-plus career (Hawks, Thunder, 76ers, Celtics and more) as a reliable stretch-big rotation piece. Solid outcome: the sleeper tag was earned — a mid-second-rounder who outproduced most of the players picked around him.

name: Marko Todorović
notes: Montenegrin big man (6'10", 250 lb) taken 45th by Portland almost entirely on size, with pre-draft evaluators already flagging that he had no standout skill — not a shooter, not a rim protector, not especially athletic or strong, and seemingly plateaued in his development. That evaluation held: Todorović never signed an NBA contract or played an NBA game, spending his entire career in Europe (Barcelona, Khimki and others), including a Spanish League title in 2014. Never an NBA player — the flagged lack of a translatable skill kept him out of the league entirely.

name: Erick Green
notes: Virginia Tech's ACC Player of the Year and the nation's leading scorer as a senior (25.0 ppg) on excellent true-shooting efficiency (.59), but scouts were explicit about the concern that would define his career: below-average lateral quickness and real doubts about guarding NBA point guards. Utah took him 46th. Green never found an NBA role — he bounced through the G League and brief NBA looks before settling into a long career overseas. Bust: an elite college scorer whose defensive limitations, flagged pre-draft, kept him off NBA rosters.

name: Raul Neto
notes: Brazilian floor general (playing in Spain's ACB) taken 47th by Atlanta and immediately dealt to Utah — a pass-first, high-IQ table-setter with a quick, compact handle and a set-shot jumper, but scouting notes flagged a tendency toward tunnel vision on some reads. Neto spent two extra years developing in Spain before joining Utah in 2015, then carved out a real, lasting NBA career as a steady backup/spot-starting point guard for the Jazz, Wizards, Sixers and Cavaliers. Solid outcome: exactly the reliable, pass-first reserve guard projected, just with a longer runway to get there.

name: Ryan Kelly
notes: Duke's senior stretch four, a skilled shooter and passer who put up a signature 36-point, 10-of-14 shooting night against Miami — the flagged weakness was a lack of foot speed and physicality to defend NBA power forwards. The Lakers took him 48th. That's almost exactly how the career played out: three seasons in LA and one in Atlanta as a floor-spacing bench piece before injuries and matchup limitations ended his run. Bust relative to a first-round-adjacent pick — never developed into more than short-term specialist depth.

name: Erik Murphy
notes: Florida senior known for accurate, high-release shooting from the power forward spot despite modest overall production — the kind of one-skill floor-spacer teams gamble on in the back of the second round. Chicago took him 49th. The gamble didn't pay off: Murphy played 24 total NBA games across two seasons (0.3/0.3) before being waived and never sticking again. Bust: the shooting skill never got enough opportunity or support around it to produce a real NBA role.

name: James Ennis III
notes: Long Beach State's Big West Player of the Year, an explosive, long-armed (7'0" wingspan) wing with high-flying athleticism and real defensive instincts, but scouts flagged him as a raw, unpolished ball-handler and shot-creator. Atlanta took him 50th and dealt him to Miami. Ennis turned into precisely that athletic, defense-first wing at the NBA level — a long, well-traveled journeyman career (Heat, Grizzlies, Pelicans, Pistons, Rockets, 76ers, Magic, Nets, Clippers) built entirely on energy, defense and finishing, never adding much shot creation. Mixed outcome: a real, decade-plus NBA career, but never more than the low-usage role player scouted.

name: Romero Osby
notes: Oklahoma senior forward who closed his college career on a tear (20.2/8.0 over his final 11 games) with a versatile scoring package, but was flagged as undersized and lacking the lateral quickness to guard either NBA forward spot. Orlando took him 51st. The defensive concern proved decisive almost immediately — Osby signed with the Magic but was waived that October without ever appearing in an NBA regular-season game. Never an NBA player: the size/defense gap identified pre-draft never closed.

name: Lorenzo Brown
notes: NC State's do-it-all junior point guard — good size (6'5"), real playmaking vision, one of the draft's best distributors — but scouts flagged persistent turnover issues and shooting inconsistency as the swing factors. Minnesota took him 52nd. Those flaws defined a short NBA run: Brown bounced through several teams as a deep backup (2.8/1.5/1.8) before his NBA career ended in 2019, continuing afterward in the G League and overseas. Bust: the size and vision were real, but the turnovers and shot inconsistency scouts flagged never got fixed enough for a lasting role.

name: Colton Iverson
notes: A Minnesota transfer who became Colorado State's defensive and rebounding anchor as a senior (9.8 boards, team-leading 25 blocks), a physical, experienced post player who had never once attempted a college three — scouts liked the toughness but projected him purely as an athletically limited backup center. Indiana took him 53rd (rights dealt to Boston). That limited developmental-big projection held: Iverson's career played out almost entirely overseas and in the G League rather than in real NBA minutes. Never a rotation NBA player — the athletic and skill-set limitations flagged pre-draft kept him off NBA rosters.

name: Arsalan Kazemi
notes: Oregon's Pac-12 All-Defensive rebounding machine (the first Iranian-born player ever drafted), a high-motor, high-IQ role forward who led the country in defensive rebounding rate — but at 6'7" with limited length and athleticism, scouts flagged that his size ruled out both shooting from the perimeter and protecting the rim, leaving an unclear NBA fit. Philadelphia took him 54th. That fit question was never resolved at the NBA level, and Kazemi's career shifted to Iran's professional league, where he became a genuine star. Never stuck in the NBA — the tweener-size concern scouts raised proved decisive.

name: Joffrey Lauvergne
notes: French big man taken 55th (Memphis, rights to Denver) on smart, opportunistic post play and good hands, but scouts were clear that despite his height he wasn't long or explosive, and needed to keep rounding out an otherwise average physical toolkit. He spent two extra years developing in Europe before debuting in 2015, and settled into a real, useful NBA run as a rotation center (Nuggets, Thunder, Bulls, Spurs) — 208 games at 5.6/3.8. Solid outcome: a lower-ceiling big who nonetheless carved out several real seasons of NBA rotation minutes.

name: Peyton Siva
notes: Louisville's championship point guard, a four-year starter and emotional floor leader who improved his decision-making every season and ran pick-and-roll as well as anyone in the draft — the flagged concern was size and toughness translating to the NBA level. Detroit took him 56th. That concern held: Siva's NBA run was brief (2.2/0.6/1.4) before his career shifted overseas by 2014. Bust as an NBA prospect, though a legitimate winning college floor general.

name: Alex Oriakhi
notes: A 2011 national champion at UConn who transferred to Missouri for his senior year (11.2/8.4), a physically strong big with real length (7'3" wingspan) — but scouts flagged him as undersized for a traditional center's skill set with no shooting range past 15 feet. Phoenix took him 57th (rights to Sacramento). That undersized-center projection held: Oriakhi's career unfolded almost entirely in the G League and overseas rather than real NBA minutes. Never stuck in the NBA — exactly the sizing mismatch flagged pre-draft.

name: Deshaun Thomas
notes: Ohio State's leading scorer as a junior (nearly 20 ppg on efficient true shooting) who could score from all three levels, but never shot better than 34.5% from three in any college season and was flagged for lackluster, below-the-rim athleticism that would hurt against NBA length. San Antonio took him 58th. The athleticism gap proved decisive at the NBA level — Thomas never appeared in a regular-season NBA game, instead building a long, successful scoring career across Europe (Nanterre, Barcelona and others) into his 30s. Never an NBA player, but a legitimate professional scorer abroad.

name: Bojan Dubljević
notes: Montenegrin stretch five starring for Valencia in Spain's ACB — the league's second-most productive scoring center, with a real face-up shooting game (47.4% from three in Liga ACB) — but scouts questioned whether his modest size and athleticism (27.5" vertical) would hold up against NBA length. Minnesota took him 59th. Dubljević chose to stay in Europe rather than test that translation, and built an outstanding 11-plus-year career with Valencia Basket, winning multiple individual and team honors. Never played in the NBA by his own choice — a European star rather than an NBA prospect who didn't pan out.

name: Jānis Timma
notes: Latvian wing taken 60th, the last pick of the draft, by Memphis — a hard-nosed, athletic slasher with a good handle and a sweet shooting stroke, but foul-prone and raw enough defensively that evaluators pegged him as a long-term draft-and-stash project. That's exactly how it played out on the NBA side: Timma never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, playing only Summer League for Memphis before his rights moved to Orlando, and instead built the bulk of his career as a productive player overseas. Never an NBA player — a draft-and-stash flier that stayed a draft-and-stash.
